83aa-artscouncil.jpg: Arts Council of Great Britain press release, embargoed Wednesday 2 November, 12 noon, headed "Ayckbourn more popular than Shakespeare: new plays attracting regional audiences; theatre audiences increasing this year; Arts Council to issue quarterly figures for regional repertory theatres". It reports that plays by Alan Ayckbourn have been attracting larger audiences in the subsidised regional theatres than those by Shakespeare, with Willie Russell in third place; that the top new plays for 1982–83 included Blood Brothers, Andy Capp, John Lennon and Restoration, the most performed of all plays being Cider with Rosie; and that after a fall in performances between 1981 and early 1983 the first two quarters of the financial year show that trend reversing, with theatres taking more at the box office in real terms than three years earlier and seats costing 20 per cent more than in 1980

mramap.jpg: Flow chart of the house as a maze: Hall at the top branching to Far Hall and Drawing Room, then down through End Hall, Music Room, Dining Room, Pantry, Conservatory, Landing, Far Landing, Bedroom, Nursery, Play Room, Wine Cellar and Cellar to Secret Room, Study, Balcony, Tower, Laundry Room, Scullery, Laboratory, Kitchen, Loft and, at the foot, Dungeon — the connections labelled Lift, Panel, Chute and Trap-door
sen-310196.jpg: Newspaper cutting headlined "Musical to open theatre", by Simon Murgatroyd, reporting that Jeeves — the musical by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Alan Ayckbourn, rewritten from the 1975 London original — will be the first production at the new £5.1m Stephen Joseph Theatre in Scarborough on 24 April, and that the old Theatre in the Round closes days earlier with Just Between Ourselves. Beside it, Theatre Development Trust press officer Wendy Saunders stands outside the converted cinema holding a placard reading "News flash: new theatre opens 24 April '96", with a portrait of Andrew Lloyd Webber below

stacks-image-565c0df-83.jpg: Page 1-2-59 of the typescript of The Sparrow. Evie asks Tony why he married a wife he does not live with, and he answers: "Ah well. It's a bit of a romantic story that. I was leaning over the Thames embankment admiring this fellow painting his house boat and I fell in and as I was coming up for the third time she dives in and pulls me out. She was nearly Junior Women's British Butterfly Stroke Champion at the time, so it was a walk over for her." Her newspaper-delivering father arrived to find her giving him the kiss of life in front of a hundred people, so they had to marry quickly — "I hardly had time to get the duckweed out of my ear"
